reference: Reusing a model pre-trained on a large source task (ImageNet, text corpus) for a target task with less data: the first layers have learned generic reusable features (edges, textures, syntax). Two modes: feature extraction (freeze the network and train a new head) or fine-tuning (retrain all or part with a small learning rate, often progressively by layers). Gains: less data, fast convergence, better performance; provided the domains are close enough.
key_points: Reuse of a pre-trained model; generic features
Extraction (frozen layers + new head) vs fine-tuning (small rate)
common_mistakes: Describing a plain copy of the model without adaptation
Fine-tuning with a high learning rate

question: What is object detection? Do you know any architectures for that?
reference: Locating and classifying several objects in an image: predicting for each a bounding box and a class. Two families: two-stage (R-CNN, Fast/Faster R-CNN: region proposals then classification, accurate), one-stage (YOLO, SSD, RetinaNet: direct prediction on a grid, fast, real time); more recently anchor-free (CenterNet, FCOS) and Transformer-based (DETR). Evaluated by mAP at different IoU thresholds.
key_points: Two-stage (Faster R-CNN) vs one-stage (YOLO, SSD, RetinaNet)

question: What is object segmentation? Do you know any architectures for that?
reference: Assigning a class to each pixel. Semantic segmentation: classes without distinguishing instances (U-Net, FCN, DeepLab with dilated convolutions, SegFormer); instance segmentation: one mask per object (Mask R-CNN, which adds a mask branch to detection); panoptic: combination of both; foundation models such as Segment Anything. Encoder-decoder architectures with skip connections to recover resolution. Evaluated by IoU / Dice.
key_points: Semantic (U-Net, DeepLab) vs instance (Mask R-CNN) vs panoptic

question: How can we use machine learning for text classification?
reference: Turn the text into a numeric representation then train a classifier. Representations: bag of words / TF-IDF (possibly n-grams) with a linear model (logistic regression, SVM) or naive Bayes; averaged word embeddings; or fine-tuning a pre-trained model (BERT and derivatives) which gives the best results today; an LLM in zero/few-shot to start without data. Pre-processing: tokenization, lowercasing, accent handling, stop words depending on the case. Evaluate with per-class precision/recall/F1, handle imbalance.
key_points: Vectorization: bag of words/TF-IDF, embeddings, pre-trained models
Suitable classifier (linear on sparse, fine-tuning on a transformer)
Per-class evaluation, imbalance; zero-shot LLM as an option
common_mistakes: Proposing gradient boosting on a huge bag of words

question: What is bag of words? How we can use it for text classification?
reference: Representation of a document by the vector of counts (or presence, or TF-IDF) of each word of the vocabulary, ignoring order. The vocabulary is built on the training corpus (CountVectorizer), you get a sparse documents x words matrix, and you train a linear classifier or naive Bayes on it. Simple, fast, interpretable (one weight per word), very effective as a baseline; loses order and context, large sparse vocabulary.
key_points: Vector of counts per word, order ignored
Vocabulary learned on train, sparse matrix
common_mistakes: Building the vocabulary on the test set
Saying the bag of words captures context

question: What are the advantages and disadvantages of bag of words?
reference: Benefits: simple to understand and implement, fast, interpretable, works well with linear models even on small corpora, solid baseline. Drawbacks: loss of order and context (negations, expressions), large vocabulary and very sparse vectors (memory, curse of dimensionality), no notion of similarity between words (orthogonal synonyms), sensitivity to typos and variants, out-of-vocabulary words in production. N-grams, TF-IDF and embeddings fix part of these limits.
key_points: High dimension, sparse, out of vocabulary
No semantic similarity between words; remedies

question: What are N-grams? How can we use them?
reference: Sequences of n consecutive elements (words or characters): unigrams, bigrams ('not good'), trigrams. Added to the bag of words, they capture some local order and expressions (negation, compound nouns); character n-grams give robustness to typos, morphology and languages without spaces. Uses: classification, statistical language models, language detection, search. Cost: exploding vocabulary (filter by minimum frequency, hashing).
key_points: Definition: sequences of n words or characters

question: How large should be N for our bag of words when using N-grams?
reference: In practice 1 to 2 or 3 for words: bigrams bring most of the gain (negations, expressions), trigrams a little more on large corpora, beyond that n-grams become too rare to generalize and the vocabulary explodes. For characters, 3 to 5. Choose by cross-validation while combining the orders (ngram_range=(1,2)) and filtering by minimum frequency; small corpus -> small N.
key_points: Combine the orders (1 to N) and filter by frequency
Choose by validation according to corpus size
common_mistakes: Proposing a high N without considering rarity
Using a single order instead of a range

question: What is TF-IDF? How is it useful for text classification?
reference: Weight of a term in a document: TF (term frequency in the document, often normalized) x IDF = log(N / number of documents containing the term). Words present everywhere ('the', 'of') get an IDF close to zero, rare and discriminative words are promoted. With L2 normalization of the vectors, it is a standard representation for linear classification and search (cosine similarity); it often improves on raw counts, especially without stop-word removal.
key_points: TF x IDF, formula and intuition
Dampens words frequent everywhere, promotes discriminative ones

question: Which model would you use for text classification with bag of words features?
reference: A linear model: logistic regression or linear SVM, with regularization, which handle high-dimensional sparse matrices very well, are fast and interpretable; multinomial naive Bayes as an even faster baseline, effective on small corpora. Trees and boosting are poorly suited (slow, inefficient on thousands of sparse columns). A simple network (fastText) is an alternative. With more data and compute, move to pre-trained models.
key_points: Why not trees on sparse data
common_mistakes: Listing representations (Word2Vec, BERT) instead of models
Proposing a random forest by default

question: Would you prefer gradient boosting trees model or logistic regression when doing text classification with bag of words?
reference: Logistic regression. The bag of words gives tens of thousands of sparse, binary or near-binary columns; a linear model exploits them directly, trains in seconds and regularizes easily. Boosting has to search for splits on each sparse column, is slow, captures combinations of rare words poorly and generally brings no accuracy gain. Boosting becomes interesting again when the dimension is reduced (embeddings, projected TF-IDF) or when text is mixed with tabular variables.
key_points: Logistic regression: high sparse dimension, speed, regularization
Boosting: slow and inefficient on sparse data
Exception: dense representations or mixed data
common_mistakes: Choosing boosting because it is 'more powerful'
Not justifying by the sparse nature of the data

question: What are word embeddings? Why are they useful? Do you know Word2Vec?
reference: Dense low-dimensional vectors (50-300) representing each word, learned so that words appearing in similar contexts have close vectors; they capture semantic and syntactic relations (king - man + woman ~ queen). Useful because they give a similarity between words, reduce the dimension and transfer knowledge from a large corpus to a small task. Word2Vec learns them with a shallow network: CBOW (predict the word from the context) or skip-gram (predict the context from the word), with negative sampling. Limit: one vector per word, independent of context (unlike BERT).
key_points: Dense vectors, close words = close contexts
Word2Vec: CBOW and skip-gram, negative sampling
common_mistakes: Saying Word2Vec is a deep or contextual model

question: Do you know any other ways to get word embeddings?
reference: GloVe (factorization of global co-occurrence statistics), fastText (subwords: handles out-of-vocabulary words and morphology), contextual embeddings from language models (ELMo, BERT and derivatives, where a word's vector depends on the sentence), embedding layers learned end to end with the task, and sentence/document embeddings (Sentence-BERT, API embedding models) for search and RAG. Historically also LSA/SVD on the term-document matrix.
common_mistakes: Confusing word embeddings with sentence embeddings

question: If you have a sentence with multiple words, you may need to combine multiple word embeddings into one. How would you do it?
reference: From simplest to most elaborate: mean (or sum, max) of the word vectors; weighted mean by IDF or by a smoothed weighting (SIF) with removal of the first principal component; concatenation of mean and max; sequential models (LSTM, CNN) or a Transformer that produce a contextual representation ([CLS] token or mean pooling), ideally trained for sentence similarity (Sentence-BERT). The mean loses order but remains a surprisingly solid baseline.
key_points: Mean / sum / max of the vectors
Sequential models or Transformer (CLS, mean pooling)
Sentence-BERT; the mean as a baseline
common_mistakes: Proposing to concatenate the vectors word by word (variable size)
Ignoring the loss of order of the mean

question: Would you prefer gradient boosting trees model or logistic regression when doing text classification with embeddings?
reference: With embeddings, the features are dense and of moderate dimension (a few hundred), and the relationships with the class are often non-linear: gradient boosting (or a small network) becomes competitive, even better, especially when embeddings are mixed with tabular variables. Logistic regression remains a fast baseline, and can be enough when the embeddings are of good quality and the task linearly separable. Test both in validation; fine-tuning the embedding model often beats both.
key_points: Dense and low dimension -> boosting relevant
Logistic regression as a fast baseline
Validate; fine-tuning the source model often superior
common_mistakes: Answering as for the bag of words

question: How can you use neural nets for text classification?
reference: Tokenize the text, convert it into a sequence of ids, pass it through an embedding layer (learned or pre-trained), then an encoder: 1D CNN over n-grams, bidirectional RNN/LSTM, or Transformer; aggregate into a vector (pooling, [CLS]) and finish with a dense layer + softmax, trained with cross-entropy. The dominant approach is fine-tuning a pre-trained model (BERT, RoBERTa, DistilBERT) with a small learning rate; regularization by dropout, early stopping; watch imbalance and maximum sequence length.
key_points: Tokenization -> embeddings -> encoder (CNN, LSTM, Transformer) -> pooling -> softmax
Fine-tuning a pre-trained model as the standard
common_mistakes: Giving a list of applications instead of the method

question: How can we use CNN for text classification?
reference: The sentence is represented as a matrix (length x embedding dimension) and 1D convolutions are applied with filters 2 to 5 words wide, which detect local patterns equivalent to learned n-grams, wherever they appear; a global max pooling over time keeps the strongest presence of each pattern; the outputs of the different widths are concatenated then passed to a dense layer with softmax (Kim's architecture, 2014). Fast, parallelisable, effective for polarity and topics; captures long dependencies less well than LSTM/Transformer.
key_points: Embedding matrix, 1D convolutions of various widths
Global max pooling then dense + softmax
common_mistakes: Describing 2D convolutions as in images without justification
Confusing it with a CNN on an image of the text

question: What is unsupervised learning?
reference: Learning structure in data without labels: grouping similar observations (clustering: K-means, DBSCAN, hierarchical), reducing dimension (PCA, t-SNE, UMAP, autoencoders), estimating densities, detecting anomalies, learning representations (self-supervision). There is no ground truth: evaluation relies on internal criteria (silhouette), stability, visualization and business usefulness. Often an exploration or pre-processing step before supervised learning.
key_points: No labels: structure, groups, dimensions, density, anomalies
Evaluation without ground truth: internal criteria, stability, usefulness
common_mistakes: Saying an accuracy can be measured

question: What is clustering? When do we need it?
reference: Partitioning observations into groups such that members of a group are similar to each other and different from the others, according to a distance or a similarity. Needs: customer or user segmentation, grouping documents or images, anomaly detection (isolated points), data compression or summary, feature creation for a supervised model, exploration before labeling. The result depends on the choice of variables, their scale, the distance and the algorithm; it is validated by internal criteria and business sense.
key_points: Homogeneous, separated groups according to a distance
Use cases: segmentation, grouping, anomalies, exploration
common_mistakes: Presenting clustering as objective rather than exploratory

question: Do you know how K-means works?
reference: Choose K and initialize K centroids (k-means++ for a good spread). Alternate: assign each point to the nearest centroid (Euclidean distance), then recompute each centroid as the mean of its points; until assignments no longer change. The algorithm minimizes inertia (sum of squared intra-cluster distances) and converges to a local optimum, hence several initializations. Assumes convex clusters of comparable sizes; sensitive to scale and outliers; K to choose.
key_points: Initialization (k-means++), then alternating assignment / mean recomputation
Objective: intra-cluster inertia; local optimum, several restarts
Assumptions: convex clusters, similar sizes, Euclidean distance
Sensitivities: scale, outliers, choice of K
common_mistakes: Swapping the steps or forgetting convergence
Believing K-means finds the global optimum

question: How to select K for K-means?
reference: Elbow method: plot inertia against K and spot the point where the gain becomes marginal (often ambiguous). Mean silhouette score (cohesion vs separation, between -1 and 1): maximize. Gap statistic (comparison with reference data without structure), stability criteria (clusters reproducible across subsamples), information criteria for Gaussian mixtures (BIC). And above all business knowledge: the number of actionable segments, the readability of the groups. Visualize (PCA/UMAP) to judge.

question: What are the other clustering algorithms do you know?
reference: K-medoids / PAM (actual medoid rather than mean, robust), agglomerative hierarchical clustering (progressive merging, dendrogram, choice of linkage criterion) or divisive, DBSCAN and HDBSCAN (density, arbitrary shapes, noise), Gaussian mixtures (probabilistic clusters, elliptical shapes, EM), mean shift, spectral clustering (similarity graph, non-convex clusters), BIRCH for very large volumes, and time-series or text clustering with suitable distances.
key_points: Choice by cluster shape, noise, volume

question: Do you know how DBScan works?
reference: Two parameters: eps (neighborhood radius) and minPts (minimum number of points within that radius). A point with at least minPts neighbors is a core point; a point in the neighborhood of a core point without being one is a border point; the others are noise. Clusters are the sets of density-connected points (chains of core points at distance <= eps). Result: number of clusters determined automatically, arbitrary shapes, noise isolated; sensitive to eps (heterogeneous densities); HDBSCAN lifts that limit.
key_points: Strengths (implicit K, shapes, noise) and limit (varying densities)
common_mistakes: Forgetting the notion of core point

question: When would you choose K-means and when DBScan?
reference: K-means: globular clusters of comparable sizes, large volume (near-linear complexity), need for interpretable centroids or to assign new points, K known or estimable. DBSCAN: arbitrary-shaped clusters, noise/outliers to isolate, unknown number of clusters, spatial data; avoid when densities vary strongly (prefer HDBSCAN), in very high dimension (uninformative distances) or on huge volumes without a spatial index. When in doubt, try both and compare silhouette and business sense.
key_points: K-means: globular, volume, centroids, known K
DBSCAN: arbitrary shapes, noise, unknown K
DBSCAN limits: varying densities, high dimension

question: What is the curse of dimensionality? Why do we care about it?
reference: As the number of dimensions grows, the volume of the space grows exponentially: data become sparse, distances between points concentrate (all points look roughly equidistant), and exponentially more observations are needed to cover the space. Consequences: distance-based methods (k-NN, clustering) unreliable, model overfitting, computational cost, visualization impossible. We care in order to choose remedies: feature selection, dimensionality reduction (PCA, UMAP), regularization, models suited to sparse data.

question: Do you know any dimensionality reduction techniques?
reference: Linear: PCA (maximum variance), SVD / LSA, factor analysis, ICA, LDA (supervised, class separation), random projections. Non-linear: t-SNE and UMAP (visualization, neighborhood preservation), kernel PCA, Isomap, autoencoders (learned representation). For text: LSA, embeddings. Distinct from feature selection (which keeps original variables). The choice depends on the goal: compression, visualization, supervised pre-processing, denoising.
key_points: Linear: PCA, SVD, LDA, random projections
Non-linear: t-SNE, UMAP, kernel PCA, autoencoders
common_mistakes: Using t-SNE as pre-processing for a model

question: What’s singular value decomposition? How is it typically used for machine learning?
reference: Any matrix X (n x p) factorises as X = U S V^T with U and V orthogonal and S diagonal with decreasing singular values. Truncating to the first k components gives the best rank-k approximation (Eckart-Young). Uses: PCA (SVD of the centered matrix: V gives the components, s^2/(n-1) the variances), LSA for text, compression and denoising, recommender systems (factorization of the users x items matrix, approximated by ALS/SGD on the known entries), stable least-squares solving, pseudo-inverse. Choose k by explained variance or scree plot.
key_points: Factorization U S V^T, singular values
Uses: PCA, LSA, compression, recommendation, least squares
common_mistakes: Mixing up singular values and eigenvalues without the link (s^2 = eigenvalues of X^T X)
Saying PCA is 'a kind of SVD' without mentioning centering

question: What is the ranking problem? Which models can you use to solve them?
reference: Ordering a set of items (documents, products) by relevance for a query or a user, the goal being the quality of the order at the top of the list rather than an absolute prediction. Approaches: pointwise (predict a relevance score per query-document pair with a regressor/classifier), pairwise (learn to order pairs: RankNet, LambdaRank, RankSVM), listwise (directly optimize a list metric: LambdaMART, ListNet). Models: gradient boosting (LambdaMART is the industry standard), neural networks, bi-encoders and cross-encoders for text. The typical pipeline has two stages: fast retrieval then reranking.
key_points: Goal: order by relevance, focus on the top of the list
common_mistakes: Treating ranking as plain binary classification without discussing the order

question: What are good unsupervised baselines for text information retrieval?
reference: BM25 (and TF-IDF with cosine similarity) on an inverted index: robust, fast, still hard to beat on lexical matches; improved by tokenization, lemmatization, weighted fields (title vs body) and query expansion. Dense search with pre-trained embeddings (Sentence-BERT, embedding models) and a vector index for semantic similarity. Hybrid search (RRF fusion of both) is a strong baseline without any training data. Evaluate on an annotated query set (nDCG, recall@k).
key_points: BM25 / TF-IDF cosine on an inverted index

question: How would you evaluate your ranking algorithms? Which offline metrics would you use?
reference: With a query set and relevance judgments (annotated or derived from clicks). Metrics: precision@k and recall@k, MRR (rank of the first relevant result), MAP (mean precision over the relevant positions), nDCG@k (position-weighted gain with graded relevance, the most used), hit rate. Compare with the baseline on the same queries, look per segment (rare, long queries), and keep in mind the biases of click-derived judgments. Complement with online evaluation (A/B, interleaving).
key_points: Comparison with the baseline per segment

question: What is precision and recall at k?
reference: Metrics computed on the top k results of a list. Precision@k = number of relevant results in the top k / k; recall@k = number of relevant results in the top k / total number of relevant results for the query. Example: 3 relevant products exist, 2 are in the top 5 -> P@5 = 2/5 = 40%, R@5 = 2/3 ~ 67%. They ignore the order inside the top k (hence MAP and nDCG) and are averaged over queries.
key_points: Ignore the order inside the top k

question: What is mean average precision at k?
reference: For one query, average precision@k is the mean of the precision@i values computed at each position i <= k where a relevant result appears (divided by the number of relevant items, or by min(k, number of relevant items)): it rewards relevant results placed early. MAP@k is the mean of AP@k over all queries. It accounts for order unlike P@k, but assumes binary relevance; nDCG generalizes to graded relevance.
key_points: AP@k: mean of the precisions at the positions of relevant items
common_mistakes: Confusing it with the mean of P@k
Forgetting that it depends on the order

question: How can we use machine learning for search?
reference: Learning to rank: a first retrieval stage (BM25, embeddings) produces candidates; a learned model reranks them from features of the query, the document and their interaction (lexical scores, semantic similarity, popularity, freshness, user signals), trained on relevance judgments or clicks with a pairwise/listwise objective (LambdaMART, neural cross-encoder). ML also serves query understanding (correction, intent classification, expansion), dense-search embeddings, personalization and diversification. Evaluate offline (nDCG) then online (A/B).
common_mistakes: Applying a learned model to the whole corpus without prior retrieval
Forgetting the source of the labels

question: How can we get training data for our ranking algorithms?
reference: Explicit judgments: human annotators rating the relevance of query-document pairs on a scale (costly, reliable, guidelines needed), possibly assisted by a calibrated LLM judge. Implicit feedback: click logs, purchases, dwell time, converted into preferences with bias correction (position, presentation). Public datasets (MS MARCO) for pre-training. Positive/negative pairs built by sampling (hard negatives from BM25). Mix the sources and validate on a clean annotated set.
key_points: Human annotation with guidelines (and LLM judge)
Clicks and implicit signals with debiasing
common_mistakes: Taking clicks as ground truth without correction

question: Can we formulate the search problem as a classification problem? How?
reference: Yes, in the pointwise approach: each (query, document) pair becomes an example with a relevant / not relevant (or graded) label, a classifier predicts a relevance probability and documents are sorted by that score. It is simple and compatible with every model, but the classification loss does not reflect the quality of the order (errors at the top of the list cost more), hence the pairwise (classify pairs: which document is better) and listwise formulations. In practice pointwise is a good baseline, often beaten by LambdaMART.
key_points: Pointwise: relevance label per pair, sort by score
Limit: the loss ignores order and position
common_mistakes: Not seeing the limit of the approach

question: How can we use clicks data as the training data for ranking algorithms?
reference: Clicks are a biased implicit signal: position bias (people click more at the top), presentation bias, trust bias, and no clicks on what was not shown. Approaches: relative preferences (a clicked document below an unclicked one is preferred, pairwise model), click models that estimate attention-corrected relevance (cascade, position-based), inverse propensity scoring weighting by the probability of being seen (estimated by interventions or swaps), satisfaction signals (reading time, conversion, last click). Always validate on annotated judgments.
key_points: Click models and inverse propensity scoring
common_mistakes: Ignoring documents that were never shown

question: Do you know how to use gradient boosting trees for ranking?
reference: With LambdaMART: gradient boosting of trees whose gradients (lambdas) are computed by pairs of documents of the same query and weighted by the nDCG change that swapping the two documents would cause; the model thus directly optimizes a list metric. Implementations (XGBoost rank:ndcg, LightGBM lambdarank, CatBoost YetiRank) take groups (one query = one group), graded relevance labels and query-document features. Usual boosting hyperparameters; evaluation by nDCG@k on a validation set grouped by query.
key_points: LambdaMART: pairwise gradients weighted by delta nDCG
Data in groups per query, graded relevance
common_mistakes: Training a pointwise regressor and calling it LambdaMART
Mixing documents of the same query between train and validation

question: How do you do an online evaluation of a new ranking algorithm?
reference: A/B test: randomly split users between the old and the new ranking and compare metrics (CTR, conversion rate, reformulations, abandonment, time to first click, revenue), with sample size and statistical test defined in advance, while monitoring guardrails (latency, revenue). Interleaving: merge the two lists in the same page and attribute clicks to each algorithm; much more sensitive, hence faster, but only measures relative preference. Progressive rollout and analysis per segment.
key_points: A/B with business metrics and guardrails, statistical power
common_mistakes: Concluding after a few days without a statistical test

question: What is a recommender system?
reference: A system that proposes to each user the items (products, films, content) most likely to interest them, from their history, other users' behavior and item attributes. Families: collaborative filtering (similarity between users or items, matrix factorization), content-based (attributes), hybrid, and two-tower neural models; candidate generation then ranking architecture. Business goals: engagement, sales, discovery, diversity; evaluated offline (precision@k, nDCG) and online (A/B).

question: What are good baselines when building a recommender system?
reference: Popularity (most viewed/purchased items, possibly per segment or period), recency, 'customers who bought X also bought Y' (co-occurrences, item-item), mean ratings with user and item biases, k-NN on items or users, simple matrix factorization (ALS). These baselines are fast, robust to cold start for popularity, and set the level to beat; a complex model that does not beat them in A/B is not justified. Also think about qualitative criteria: relevance, novelty, diversity.

question: What is collaborative filtering?
reference: Predicting a user's interest in an item from the interactions (ratings, clicks, purchases) of all users, without describing the content of the items: 'those who liked what you like also liked...'. Variants: memory-based (user-user or item-item k-NN with cosine/Pearson similarity, weighted mean of ratings after per-user centering) and model-based (matrix factorization: users and items projected into a latent space, ALS, SGD, SVD++, or networks). Strengths: only needs the interaction matrix, improves with usage; limits: sparse matrix, cold start, popularity bias.
key_points: Prediction from others' interactions, without content

question: How we can incorporate implicit feedback (clicks, etc) into our recommender systems?
reference: Implicit feedback has no explicit negatives: the absence of interaction can mean disinterest or non-exposure, and the intensity (number of clicks, duration) reflects confidence rather than a rating. Approaches: confidence-weighted matrix factorization (Hu, Koren & Volinsky, implicit ALS: all unobserved pairs count as weak negatives), pairwise learning (BPR: an interacted item is preferred over a sampled non-interacted one), two-tower models with negative sampling, correction of position and exposure biases, and weighting of actions by value (purchase > click).
common_mistakes: Treating the absence of interaction as a certain 0 rating

question: What is the cold start problem?
reference: The inability of collaborative filtering to recommend when interactions are missing: new user (no history, so no similarity nor latent factors), new item (nobody has rated or clicked it yet, it cannot be recommended collaboratively), or even a new system without data. Consequences: generic or absent recommendations, new items invisible (popularity vicious circle).
key_points: Cases: new user, new item, new system
Consequences: generic recommendations, new items invisible
common_mistakes: Citing only one of the two cases
Confusing it with the service's slow start-up

question: Possible approaches to solving the cold start problem?
reference: New item: content-based recommendation (attributes, description, text/image embeddings) or hybrid models combining content and collaboration; exploration (show the new item to a sample of users, bandits); editorial promotion. New user: onboarding questionnaire about tastes, demographic or contextual data, popularity per segment, recommendations based on the current session, bandits to learn fast. In every case, switch progressively to collaborative filtering as interactions arrive.
key_points: Users: onboarding, demographics, session, popularity per segment

question: What is a time series?
reference: A sequence of observations ordered in time, generally at regular intervals (daily sales, hourly temperature, traffic per minute). Its particularity: observations are dependent (autocorrelation) and the series may show trend, seasonality, cycles and noise; the order is information, methods assuming independence do not apply as is. Tasks: forecasting, anomaly detection, decomposition, series classification.
key_points: Observations ordered in time, regular step

question: How is time series different from the usual regression problem?
reference: In classic regression the observations are assumed independent and identically distributed, and y is predicted from explanatory variables. In time series, observations are correlated in time, the target depends on its own past values, and the distribution can change (non-stationarity, trend, seasonality). Consequences: lagged variables and rolling windows, validation respecting temporal order (no random shuffling), metrics per horizon, and dedicated models (ARIMA, exponential smoothing) or adaptation of classic models with temporal features.
key_points: Target depends on its past, non-stationarity
common_mistakes: Saying explanatory variables cannot be used

question: Which models do you know for solving time series problems?
reference: Baselines: naive (last value), seasonal naive, moving average. Exponential smoothing: simple, Holt (trend), Holt-Winters (trend + seasonality), ETS. ARIMA/SARIMA models (autoregression, differencing, moving average) and with exogenous variables (SARIMAX), vector models (VAR). Decomposition (STL) and Prophet. Machine learning on temporal features (lags, windows, calendar): regression, gradient boosting. Deep learning: RNN/LSTM, TCN, temporal Transformers, N-BEATS; foundation models for series. Choose by volume, seasonalities, horizon, exogenous variables.
key_points: ML on temporal features, deep learning

question: If there’s a trend in our series, how we can remove it? And why would we want to do it?
reference: Methods: differencing (y_t - y_{t-1}, possibly seasonal), regressing the series on time then working on the residuals, decomposition (STL) to isolate trend and seasonality, log transformation for a multiplicative trend, or explicit modeling (Holt, ARIMA with differencing term d). Why: many models (ARIMA, autocorrelations, tests) assume stationarity (constant mean and variance); without it estimates and forecasts are biased, and spurious correlations appear between trending series. The trend is reintegrated for the final forecast.
key_points: Differencing, regression on time, decomposition, log
Reintegrate the trend in the forecast

question: You have a series with only one variable “y” measured at time t. How do predict “y” at time t+1? Which approaches would you use?
reference: Exploit autocorrelation: start with baselines (last value, seasonal naive), then univariate models: exponential smoothing (Holt-Winters if seasonal), ARIMA/SARIMA after ACF/PACF analysis and differencing, or a machine learning model on features built from the past (lags y_{t-1..t-k}, rolling means, calendar). Validate with a temporal split (rolling origin) on the one-step-ahead error, compare with the baselines, and forecast with an uncertainty interval.
key_points: ML on lags and rolling windows
common_mistakes: Using future information in the features

question: You have a series with a variable “y” and a set of features. How do you predict “y” at t+1? Which approaches would you use?
reference: Combine the past of y and the exogenous variables: ARIMAX/SARIMAX models or dynamic regression, or more commonly a machine learning model (gradient boosting, regularized regression) on features: lags and rolling statistics of y, exogenous variables known at forecast time (beware of using future values; if a variable is only known afterwards, forecast it or lag it), calendar, events. Deep learning (LSTM, Transformers) with lots of data and series. Temporal-split validation, comparison with univariate models to check that the variables add something.
key_points: ML on lags of y + exogenous + calendar
Availability of exogenous variables at forecast time (leakage)
common_mistakes: Using exogenous variables measured at t+1

question: What are the problems with using trees for solving time series problems?
reference: Trees predict with leaf means: they cannot extrapolate beyond the range of training values, so they miss a rising trend or never-seen levels (they plateau). They have no notion of order: lags, windows and calendar variables must be built explicitly, and leakage avoided. Remedies: remove the trend first (predict differences or ratios, detrend then reintegrate), combine with a linear model, or use models that extrapolate. Once these precautions are taken, gradient boosting performs very well.
key_points: No extrapolation outside the training range
No notion of order: explicit features, leakage
Still performs well with these precautions
